patient.chief_complaint: Persistent neck pain and stiffness for 15 days with near-syncopal episode today
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Gerald Novak is a 59-year-old right-handed retired warehouse manager who presents to the emergency department after a near-syncopal episode earlier today. His symptoms began 15 days ago with the insidious onset of neck stiffness, which he initially attributed to sleeping in an awkward position. He visited his primary care physician five days into his symptoms and was prescribed methocarbamol for presumed musculoskeletal neck pain. Despite the muscle relaxant, his symptoms did not improve. Two days later, he presented to this emergency department reporting involuntary contractions of the neck muscles causing his head to be held in left rotation. At that initial ED visit, he denied headache, photophobia, fever, nausea, vomiting, upper-extremity weakness or numbness, stridor, dysphagia, drooling, odynophagia, or respiratory symptoms. He had no history of trauma. He was afebrile with normal vital signs, and imaging of the head and cervical spine was obtained. He reported significant pain relief after receiving intramuscular ketorolac and was discharged with Tylenol #3 and instructions for primary care follow-up. Four days later he returned to the ED with persistent neck pain. He remained afebrile, his examination was unchanged, and he was treated with ketorolac and discharged with acetaminophen/hydrocodone, cyclobenzaprine, and ibuprofen. Today, six days after his second ED visit, he experienced a near-syncopal episode upon standing from a seated position. He reports feeling dizzy and lightheaded, which he attributes to the cyclobenzaprine. He again denies headache, fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting. His wife reports that he has seemed more fatigued over the past several days and has had a poor appetite. She notes that his neck has remained persistently stiff and twisted despite multiple medications. On arrival to the ED, he is tachycardic at 120 beats per minute but afebrile.

results.title: Invasive Group B Streptococcal Disease in Nonpregnant Adults
results.authors: Farley MM, Harvey RC, Stull T, et al.
results.key_finding: GBS disease in nonpregnant adults is associated with diabetes mellitus, liver disease, malignancy, and advanced age. Meningitis accounts for approximately 4% of invasive GBS disease in adults.

results.title: Group B Streptococcal Meningitis in Adults: A Systematic Review
results.authors: van Kassel MN, Bijlsma MW, Brouwer MC, et al.
results.key_finding: Adult GBS meningitis has a case fatality rate of 15-27%. Diabetes mellitus is the most common comorbidity. Treatment with high-dose penicillin G or ampicillin for 14-21 days is recommended. Some experts add gentamicin for synergy during the first 5-7 days.

results.title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis
results.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, et al.
results.key_finding: For GBS meningitis, recommended treatment is penicillin G 4 million units IV every 4 hours or ampicillin 2g IV every 4 hours for 14-21 days. Adjunctive dexamethasone evidence is strongest for pneumococcal meningitis; benefit in GBS meningitis is less established.

output.summary: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) meningitis in nonpregnant adults is uncommon but carries significant mortality (15-27%). Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, advanced age, liver disease, and immunosuppression. The role of adjunctive dexamethasone is less established for GBS meningitis compared to pneumococcal meningitis. Skin and soft-tissue breaks are recognized portals of entry for GBS bacteremia in adult populations.

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture with opening-pressure measurement and send CSF for cell count with differential, glucose (with paired serum), protein, Gram stain, bacterial culture, meningitis multiplex PCR panel, and CSF lactate.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Elevated opening pressure, PMN-predominant pleocytosis, low CSF:serum glucose ratio (<0.4), elevated protein, elevated CSF lactate; PCR or culture identifies the organism.

useless_tools.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60). LP performed in undetected mass effect can precipitate fatal herniation.

Blood cultures must be drawn (under interpret_labs) before the first dose of empiric antibiotics so that culture yield is not lost; in practice this means peripheral cultures are collected at the same draw as the CSF analysis is initiated, and the lab tube sequencing prevents antibiotic exposure before specimen acquisition.

critical_actions: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
Do NOT assume a benign musculoskeletal etiology for fluctuating neck stiffness in older or immunocompromised patients without first excluding meningitis with LP.
key_reasoning_points: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.
Group B Streptococcus is unusual in non-pregnant adults; risk factors include diabetes, age >60, malignancy, and cirrhosis. Coverage with ampicillin (or penicillin) plus ceftriaxone is appropriate.
